story_text.value:
Hey everyone, SideKernel is the result of my capstone project for my MSc at Georgia Tech.

There are a lot of sandboxes on the market right now for AI agents, but most of them focus on production deployments, rather than coding agents (e.g. Claude Code).

I always felt uncomfortable running Claude Code or other coding agents directly on my machine, and I didn't want to buy a second computer or rent a VPS just for that.

That's why I made SideKernel: a sandbox that tries to be as transparent as possible to the everyday developer.

I hope you find some value in it, and feedback is more than welcome. Usability is hard to get right without large user studies, so I'd really value hearing about any annoyances or blockers you run into.

Thanks!

story_text.value:
I’ve been working on AppMaker, a small experiment in visual app development.

It has a visual UI builder, JavaScript on both the client and server, a built-in database, and lets you download the generated Node.js app.

It’s still early, and I’m especially curious about one thing: In the age of AI coding tools, is there still a place for this kind of structured visual development environment??!!?!

I’d genuinely appreciate feedback, including criticism.

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I've been a heavy user of coding agents for over a year now, and while excited by the productivity gains - I've increasingly been frustrated at the process around it.

- Prompts are imperative and ephemeral, and code is increasingly a black-box, so I lose track of intent over long horizons.

- Pull requests, CI/CD, and even GitHub have become process bottlenecks and are increasingly losing meaning in a world of code abundance.

- I'm tired of babysitting coding agents, cleaning up slop, and reviewing AI output!

I've been building Telos to solve some of these problems - it's a new, declarative abstraction layer for building software with AI. We treat the goal specification as the source of truth that AI coding agents continuously reconcile against in a cloud environment.

We've been dogfooding this quietly for a few months, and it's solved many of the problems above for us - we're excited to share this with the world!

Our agent runtime's source is available [0], and instructions to try it out alongside a real-world example are at the end of the linked post.

Cheers

[0] https://github.com/telos-org/telos

story_text.value:
I've been working on Yengi for several months. I am a teacher, not a professional software developer. My path here started with Microsoft Small Basic, Scratch, and MIT App Inventor, which I used to teach children.

I originally started it for a simple reason: I was using VS Code + Copilot, Trae, Cursor and Google Antigravity, and I kept running into usage limits and provider-specific workflows.

I wanted something where I could choose my own model or API, including local models running through Ollama, and build without being tied to one provider.

It grew considerably beyond that original idea.

Yengi is a .NET 10 / WPF desktop application with:

* Agent and tool system for files, terminal, Git, builds and tests * RAG and LSP integration * Verification loops with checkpoints and rollback * 30+ agent tools * Support for local models and external APIs * A custom 1.5B router model that I fine-tuned on thousands of examples of Yengi-specific agent decisions * 200+ automated tests

It also has three additional modes besides the coding environment:

*Blender:* Yengi can communicate with Blender, generate `bpy` scripts, keep conversational scene context, and optionally inspect Blender viewport screenshots through a multimodal model. I also added an optional prompt-engineering layer. For example, "create a low-poly tree" is expanded into a more detailed 3D-oriented instruction before being sent to the model. A follow-up such as "add five red apples to this tree" can modify the existing scene rather than starting from scratch.

*Unity:* Yengi can work with Unity projects, generate C# components and interact with the Unity Editor.

*Image generation:* Images can be generated from the development environment and saved directly into the project.

The unusual part is how I built it.

I used AI coding tools heavily, particularly Google Antigravity and GitHub Copilot. I didn't manually type the majority of the C# code.

My role was primarily architecture, agent behavior, security boundaries, verification and rollback logic, router training, testing, debugging AI-generated changes, and integrating the different systems.

I'm still trying to figure out how much of this approach is genuinely useful and how much is me having fun building increasingly complicated things.

The project is free and open source under AGPL-3.0:

https://github.com/mdaiWorks/yengi

I'd especially like feedback from people working with .NET/C#, coding agents, local models, Blender or Unity.

In particular, I'm curious about:

* Is a small fine-tuned local router actually useful for this kind of agent? * Does the verification/rollback architecture make sense? * Are the Blender/Unity integrations useful beyond being demos? * If you were building this, what would you simplify or change?

I'm not trying to claim that this replaces VS Code or Cursor. I'm interested in whether this particular approach is useful at all, and what I should change next.

story_text.value:
Hi! I am Hussain and I built Caspian.

For someone who vibe builds almost all the time, for both personal tools like investment or health dashboards or tools to help others, I found my projects scattered all over the place: researching with claude, writing context in notion, building with Claude Code, Devin, publishing in vercel, posthog for analytics and then others tools for GTM. Big part of brain energy drain was context switching, I wasn't very organized.

So I decided to build that lets me do all this from one place. I built Caspian. While most AI coding tools you use for vibe building stop at code, Caspian takes it all the way to users.

Caspian creates a "workbench" folder in your local machine where it puts all your projects so everything stays in one place and is also easy for your other tools to work with. There is a built in co-pilot, a context manager (.md files user can copilot both read/write), a one click publisher, analytics and an email outreach manager. Though the copilot uses API for processing LLM requests via open router (I make a little margin on top), it is pricy, so I build a standard "canvas" format that Caspian uses that your Claude/Codex or other tools you use also understand and can work with. Simply point them to https://caspian.md/docs and they'll learn to work with Caspian straight away, this is so that you're not tied to Caspian's co-pilot and if you prefer to use your own tools, you can do so.

Some other features I built around problems i found myself struggle with:

- Prompt refinement: Enter a vague prompt in co-pilot, caspian uses a cheap model to generate a detailed before starting the task.

- Preflight: It breaks down the task and tells you estimatedly, how much will it cost and how long will it take, before starting the task.

- Product and User context: Co-pilot has access to the two files so both you and Caspain has understand of your product and user.

- Code/No code: You can switch this button to dive into code or just stick with the vibes.

I hope it helps and you can build and launch a lot quickly. Feedback what's the most annoying thing when you vibe code?

title.value: Show HN: Caspian – Desktop app to build and launch small vibe-coded projects
